questions.question: How do you design and run performance tests for a Java backend service — what's the difference between load, stress, soak, and spike tests, and how do you act on the results?
questions.title: Performance Testing for Java Backends: Load, Stress, Soak, Spike
questions.direct_answer: Performance testing is **not one thing** — it's a family of tests that answer different questions: **load** ('does it handle expected traffic?'), **stress** ('where does it break?'), **soak** ('does it degrade over time — leaks, GC pressure?'), **spike** ('how does it react to sudden bursts?'), and **capacity** ('what's our headroom?'). For Java backends: define **SLOs** (p50/p95/p99 latency, error rate, throughput) **before** testing, model realistic load with a tool (k6, Gatling, JMeter, Locust), run against a **prod-like environment** with prod-like data, and **profile** during the run (JFR, async-profiler, Prometheus, JVM metrics). The goal isn't pretty graphs — it's **identifying the bottleneck** (CPU, GC, DB, network, lock contention) and fixing it iteratively. Common pitfalls: testing in dev / shared envs (unreliable), measuring averages instead of percentiles (hides tail latency), no thread-pool / connection-pool tuning during the run, comparing across JVM warmup states, and treating one-off runs as definitive (use trend analysis instead). Best practice: **continuous performance testing** in CI, performance budgets per service, and load tests as part of release gates for high-traffic services.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of different perf test types; ability to design tests with SLOs; debugging perf bottlenecks in JVM/Spring
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Confusing perf test types; using averages; testing in shared envs; one-off runs without trend
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Discuss SLO-driven testing, JFR / async-profiler, JVM warmup, p99 latency, continuous perf testing, capacity planning

sections.title: The Family of Performance Tests
sections.content:
**Performance testing** is an umbrella for several distinct test types, each answering a different question. Conflating them is the #1 cause of useless 'perf tests' in the wild.

- **Load test**: Does the system meet SLOs at expected production load? (e.g., 1000 RPS for 30 min, p99 < 200ms)
- **Stress test**: At what point does the system break? Find the **knee of the curve** — throughput plateaus, latency spikes, errors appear
- **Soak test (endurance)**: Does the system degrade over hours/days? Detects memory leaks, connection leaks, GC pressure buildup, log file growth, slow DB query plans
- **Spike test**: How does the system react to sudden bursts? E.g., 10x normal traffic for 1 minute. Tests autoscaling, queue saturation, recovery
- **Capacity test**: What's our headroom? At current traffic, are we at 30% or 80% of capacity? Drives infrastructure / scaling decisions
- **Smoke / sanity perf test**: Quick run to verify nothing massively regressed; lightweight; CI-friendly

**The common goal**: characterize how the system behaves under load — not just average response time, but **percentiles** (p50, p95, p99, p99.9), **error rates**, **throughput**, and **resource utilization** (CPU, memory, GC, DB connections, thread pools).

**Why this matters**: production traffic isn't average. Tail latency (p99, p99.9) defines user experience; one slow request matters more than 99 fast ones for a user who has to wait.

sections.title: Performance Test Types Compared
sections.content:
| Type | Goal | Duration | Load shape | Pass criteria |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Smoke** | Nothing broken | 5–10 min | Light, steady | All requests succeed; rough latency in range |
| **Load** | Meets SLO at expected load | 30–60 min | Steady, target RPS | p99 < SLO; error rate < SLO; throughput stable |
| **Stress** | Find breaking point | Until failure | Ramp up indefinitely | Identify knee of curve; no crashes (graceful degradation) |
| **Soak** | Long-term stability | Hours to days | Steady, moderate | No memory growth; no connection leak; latency stable |
| **Spike** | Burst tolerance | 10–30 min | Sudden 5–10x burst | Recovery time; no cascading failure; autoscale works |
| **Capacity** | Headroom analysis | 30–60 min per level | Stepped ramp | Utilization at expected load < target (e.g., 70%) |

sections.title: Designing and Running Load Tests for Spring Boot
Acting on Results: Bottlenecks and Fixes
sections.content:
**Read the percentiles, not the average**

```
Avg latency: 50ms      → looks great
p50: 30ms              → most users
p95: 100ms             → 5% slower
p99: 800ms             → 1% catastrophically slow
p99.9: 3000ms          → 1 in 1000 timing out
```

The average lies. The tail tells the story. **Latency at p99 / p99.9 is what users feel during incidents.**

**Common bottlenecks and how to spot them:**

| Bottleneck | Symptom | Tool to confirm | Fix direction |
|---|---|---|---|
| CPU bound | High CPU, low DB / network usage | JFR CPU profile | Optimize hot path; cache; algorithmic fix |
| GC pressure | High GC time %, frequent pauses | GC logs, JFR alloc profile | Reduce allocation; bigger heap; G1 → ZGC |
| DB slow query | High DB CPU / slow query log | Postgres pg_stat_statements | Index, query plan, denormalize |
| Connection pool exhaustion | Latency spikes when RPS rises | HikariCP metrics | Increase pool; reduce hold time |
| Thread pool saturation | Tomcat thread pool full; requests queue | Micrometer thread metrics | Increase max threads; async; virtual threads |
| Lock contention | High CPU but low throughput; lock wait time | JFR lock contention | Reduce critical section; lock striping; lock-free |
| Network / external API | High latency on specific endpoints; downstream slow | Distributed tracing | Cache; circuit breaker; bulkhead; parallelize |
| Memory leak | Heap grows over soak; OOM eventually | Heap dump; Eclipse MAT | Find root reference; fix lifecycle |
| Cache miss | High DB load with cache enabled | Cache hit rate metric | Pre-warm; increase TTL; size up |

**Iterative tuning loop:**
1. Run perf test → capture baseline
2. Identify the **#1 bottleneck** (don't try to fix everything at once)
3. Hypothesize fix
4. Apply fix in code or config
5. Re-run perf test → compare
6. If improved, move to next bottleneck; if not, revisit hypothesis

Keep a **performance journal**: each run, what changed, what improved, what regressed.

**Soak test specifics:**
- Run 4–24 hours at moderate load
- Watch heap usage trend, file descriptors, DB connections, log volume
- A leak shows as **monotonic growth that GC can't reclaim**
- Capture heap dump at start and end; compare in Eclipse MAT or VisualVM

**Spike test specifics:**
- Sudden ramp (e.g., 0 → 5000 RPS in 30 sec)
- Watch: does autoscaler trigger? How fast? Does the queue absorb? Does any downstream cascade fail?
- Recovery time is as important as peak handling — system should normalize within seconds after spike ends

**Stress test specifics:**
- Ramp until failure
- The 'knee of the curve': latency rises sharply, throughput plateaus, errors begin
- This is your **maximum capacity** number — plan headroom (typically run at 50–70% of capacity in production)
- System should fail **gracefully** — 503s, circuit breakers tripping, not crashes / OOM / cascading failures

**Continuous performance testing:**
- Run a smoke perf test in CI on every merge (5–10 min)
- Run full load test on staging deploys
- Establish **performance budgets** per service: 'this endpoint must handle X RPS at p99 < Y'
- **Trend analysis**: regression detection over time; alert when a deploy causes >10% perf degradation
- Tools: k6 Cloud, Grafana Cloud k6, Datadog Synthetic monitoring, BlazeMeter

**Anti-patterns:**
1. **Testing in dev** — unreliable; results don't reflect production
2. **Reporting averages** — hides tail; use percentiles
3. **Single client machine** — client becomes bottleneck before SUT does
4. **No warmup** — JIT cold start corrupts data
5. **Unrealistic data** — 100-row test DB hides query plan issues at scale
6. **No monitoring during test** — you see results but not why
7. **One-off runs** — perf tests should be repeatable, comparable
8. **Testing only happy path** — stress error paths too (validation failures, 404s)
9. **No SLOs** — 'is this fast enough?' with no answer
10. **Optimization without measurement** — 'this should be faster' = guess; prove it

sections.title: Strategic Considerations and Common Challenges
sections.content:
**Tooling choice:**
- **k6**: modern, scriptable in JS, great cloud option, easy to embed in CI; my default for new projects
- **Gatling**: excellent for JVM teams; Java/Kotlin/Scala DSL; great reports; integrates well with Maven/Gradle
- **JMeter**: GUI + XML config; mature; many plugins; verbose; my least favorite for code-as-config workflows
- **Locust**: Python-based; great for teams with Python skills
- **Vegeta**: simple Go-based HTTP load gen; quick smoke tests
- **wrk / wrk2**: low-level HTTP benchmarking; great for simple endpoints; less for complex flows

**Coordinated vs uncoordinated omission:**
- Most tools (JMeter default, naive k6) suffer from **coordinated omission**: when a request takes long, subsequent requests aren't sent until it finishes, hiding latency
- Use tools that issue requests at fixed rate regardless of response (Gatling open model, k6 with `executor: constant-arrival-rate`, wrk2)
- Otherwise, p99 numbers are dramatically optimistic

**Java-specific considerations:**

*JIT warmup*
- HotSpot recompiles hot code; first runs are slower
- Allow 1–2 min warmup at low load before measurement

*GC tuning*
- GC pause is a major contributor to latency outliers
- For low-latency: G1 (default), ZGC, Shenandoah (sub-millisecond pauses on large heaps)
- Tune `-Xms` = `-Xmx` (avoid resize)
- Watch GC time as % of CPU; > 5% is problematic

*Virtual threads (JDK 21+)*
- Game-changer for IO-bound workloads in Spring Boot 3.2+
- Removes thread pool as bottleneck for blocking IO
- Test with both platform threads and virtual threads; results vary by workload

*Connection pools*
- HikariCP default pool size (10) is often too low for high-RPS services
- Tune based on `db_concurrency = (core_count * 2) + effective_spindle_count` (rough heuristic)
- Watch HikariCP `pendingThreads` metric — non-zero = pool too small

**Capacity planning:**
- Run capacity tests at expected load × 1.5–2x (room for growth + safety margin)
- Capacity ≠ max throughput; capacity = max throughput at acceptable latency
- Use results to size infrastructure and set autoscaler thresholds

**Microservices challenges:**
- Performance test individual services in isolation
- Then test critical user flows end-to-end
- Identify which services become bottlenecks first under load
- One slow downstream can cascade; bulkheads / circuit breakers prevent

**Database load:**
- DB is the most common bottleneck in high-RPS systems
- Test with **realistic data volume and distribution**; not 1000 rows
- Watch query plans (postgres `EXPLAIN ANALYZE`)
- Connection pool sizing critical; tune at DB layer (`max_connections`) and app layer (HikariCP)
- Consider read replicas, caching, denormalization, and async writes

**Cache effects:**
- First N requests fill cache; subsequent ones hit cache; latency drops
- Decide what you're testing: cold cache or warm cache?
- Cache eviction under load can cause sudden latency spikes

**Production validation:**
- Synthetic monitoring continuously runs key flows in production
- Real User Monitoring (RUM) captures actual user latency
- Sometimes perf bugs only show in production traffic patterns
- Canary deploys with extra monitoring catch perf regressions before full rollout

**Performance testing isn't a one-time activity:**
- Continuous: every merge runs smoke perf
- Periodic: full load tests on releases
- Pre-event: extra capacity tests before known traffic spikes (Black Friday, marketing campaigns)
- Reactive: when perf incident happens, reproduce and fix

**Strategic take:**
- Pick the right test type for the question you're answering
- Define SLOs first, measure against them
- Test in prod-like envs with prod-like data
- Profile and observe during the run, not just at the end
- Iterate on bottlenecks, one at a time
- Embrace continuous performance testing as you would unit tests
- Tail latency is what users feel; p99 / p99.9 is the real number

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- Performance testing isn't one thing: **load**, **stress**, **soak**, **spike**, **capacity** answer different questions
- Define **SLOs first** (p99 latency, error rate, throughput) before designing tests
- Use modern tools: **k6**, **Gatling**, **JMeter**, **Locust**
- Test against **prod-like env** with prod-like data, never dev or shared envs
- **Warm up the JVM** before measurement; JIT compilation matters
- Measure **percentiles (p50, p95, p99, p99.9)**, not averages — the average lies
- Profile during the run: **JFR**, **async-profiler**, Prometheus, JVM metrics
- Common bottlenecks: CPU, GC pressure, DB queries, connection pool, thread pool, lock contention, downstream APIs
- **Soak tests** find leaks; **spike tests** test autoscale + recovery; **stress tests** find max capacity
- **Continuous performance testing** in CI; performance budgets per service
- Avoid **coordinated omission** (use open models, not closed)
- Capacity = max throughput **at acceptable latency**, not raw max

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
Performance testing is not one thing — it's a family of tests answering different questions.

**Test types**
- Load: does it handle expected traffic?
- Stress: where does it break?
- Soak: does it degrade over time — leaks, GC pressure?
- Spike: how does it react to sudden bursts?
- Capacity: what's our headroom?

**For Java backends**
- Define SLOs (p50/p95/p99 latency, error rate, throughput) before testing
- Model realistic load with k6, Gatling, JMeter, Locust
- Run against prod-like environment with prod-like data
- Profile during the run (JFR, async-profiler, Prometheus, JVM metrics)
- Goal: identify bottleneck (CPU, GC, DB, network, lock) and fix iteratively

**Pitfalls**
- Testing in dev/shared envs (unreliable)
- Measuring averages instead of percentiles (hides tail latency)
- No thread/connection pool tuning during run
- Comparing across JVM warmup states
- One-off runs as definitive (use trend analysis)

**Best practice**
- Continuous perf testing in CI
- Performance budgets per service
- Load tests as release gates for high-traffic services

**The family in detail**
- Smoke: nothing broken, 5-10 min, light steady
- Load: meets SLO at expected, 30-60 min, steady target RPS, p99 < SLO + error rate < SLO + stable throughput
- Stress: find break point, until failure, ramp indefinitely, identify knee + no crashes (graceful degrade)
- Soak: long-term stability, hours-days, steady moderate, no memory growth + no connection leak + stable latency
- Spike: burst tolerance, 10-30 min, sudden 5-10x, recovery time + no cascading + autoscale works
- Capacity: headroom, 30-60 min/level, stepped ramp, utilization at expected < target (70%)

**Common goal**
- Characterize behavior under load
- Not just average response time
- Percentiles (p50, p95, p99, p99.9), error rates, throughput, resource utilization (CPU, mem, GC, DB conn, thread pools)

**Why it matters**
- Production traffic isn't average
- Tail latency (p99, p99.9) defines user experience
- One slow request matters more than 99 fast for the user waiting

**Designing load tests for Spring Boot**

*1. Define SLOs first*
- Don't run without knowing 'pass'
- Example: p99 < 200ms, error < 0.1%, sustained 500 RPS
- Derive from product requirements, not 'whatever current is'

*2. Build realistic traffic profile*
- Mix of operations (80% reads, 15% writes, 5% updates) mirror production
- Think time (realistic pause between requests; without = over-saturate)
- Distribution (parameterized data, CSV of IDs; not all hit same record)
- Auth (real flow, not bypass; tokens cost CPU)
- Payload sizes realistic, not minimal

*3. Tools*
- k6: modern, JS-scriptable, great cloud option, CI-friendly; my default
- Gatling: excellent for JVM teams; Java/Kotlin/Scala DSL; great reports
- JMeter: GUI + XML; mature; many plugins; verbose
- Locust: Python-based
- Vegeta: simple Go HTTP load gen for quick smoke
- wrk/wrk2: low-level HTTP benchmark; simple endpoints

*k6 example essentials*
- options.stages: ramp up + sustain + ramp down
- thresholds: p(99)<200, http_req_failed rate<0.001
- check + sleep with random think time
- tags for endpoint-level breakdown

*Gatling: Simulation class with rampUsersPerSec/constantUsersPerSec, assertions on responseTime().percentile(99).lt(200)*

*4. Prod-like environment*
- Same instance sizes, network topology, DB sizing
- Realistic data volume (millions, not 100)
- Same Java version, GC config, container limits
- Don't share (noisy neighbor)
- Ideally ephemeral env per run

*5. Warm up JVM first*
- JIT compilation matters
- Run low-load warmup phase (1-2 min) before measurement
- Discard those numbers
- stages: 2m@50 (warmup) + 5m@500 (measure)

*6. Profile during run*
- JVM: heap, GC time, GC frequency, threads (Micrometer + Prometheus)
- App: request rate, latency by endpoint, error rate, queue depths
- DB: connection pool usage, slow queries, lock waits, replication lag
- Infra: CPU, mem, network, disk IO
- Profiler: JFR or async-profiler for CPU/alloc/lock hotspots
- jcmd <pid> JFR.start name=loadtest duration=15m filename=loadtest.jfr
- View in JDK Mission Control or JFR Analyzer

**Reading results**

*Read percentiles, not average*
- Avg 50ms looks great but masks tail
- p50 30ms, p95 100ms, p99 800ms, p99.9 3000ms
- Average lies; tail tells story
- p99/p99.9 is what users feel during incidents

*Common bottlenecks*
| Bottleneck | Symptom | Tool | Fix |
| CPU bound | High CPU, low DB/net | JFR CPU profile | Optimize hot path, cache, algo |
| GC pressure | High GC time %, frequent pauses | GC logs, JFR alloc | Reduce alloc; bigger heap; G1→ZGC |
| DB slow query | High DB CPU/slow log | pg_stat_statements | Index, query plan, denormalize |
| Connection pool | Latency spikes when RPS rises | HikariCP metrics | Increase pool; reduce hold time |
| Thread pool | Tomcat full; requests queue | Micrometer thread metrics | Increase max; async; virtual threads |
| Lock contention | High CPU low throughput | JFR lock contention | Reduce critical section; striping; lock-free |
| Network/external | High latency on specific endpoints | Tracing | Cache; circuit breaker; bulkhead; parallelize |
| Memory leak | Heap grows over soak; OOM eventually | Heap dump + Eclipse MAT | Find root reference; fix lifecycle |
| Cache miss | High DB load with cache | Cache hit rate metric | Pre-warm; increase TTL; size up |

*Iterative tuning loop*
1. Run perf test → baseline
2. Identify #1 bottleneck (don't fix all at once)
3. Hypothesize fix
4. Apply in code/config
5. Re-run → compare
6. If improved, move to next; else revisit hypothesis
- Keep performance journal: each run, what changed, what improved/regressed

**Specifics by test type**

*Soak*
- 4-24 hours moderate load
- Watch heap trend, file descriptors, DB connections, log volume
- Leak = monotonic growth GC can't reclaim
- Heap dump at start + end, compare in MAT/VisualVM

*Spike*
- Sudden ramp (0→5000 RPS in 30s)
- Watch: autoscaler trigger? How fast? Queue absorbs? Downstream cascade?
- Recovery time as important as peak handling
- Should normalize within seconds after spike

*Stress*
- Ramp until failure
- Knee of curve: latency rises sharply, throughput plateaus, errors begin
- Maximum capacity number; plan headroom (run at 50-70% of capacity)
- Should fail gracefully (503s, breakers tripping; not crashes/OOM/cascading)

**Continuous perf testing**
- Smoke perf in CI every merge (5-10 min)
- Full load on staging deploys
- Performance budgets per service: 'this endpoint must handle X RPS at p99 < Y'
- Trend analysis: regression detection; alert on >10% degradation per deploy
- Tools: k6 Cloud, Grafana Cloud k6, Datadog Synthetic, BlazeMeter

**Anti-patterns**
1. Testing in dev (unreliable)
2. Reporting averages (hides tail)
3. Single client machine (client becomes bottleneck)
4. No warmup (JIT cold start corrupts data)
5. Unrealistic data (100-row hides query plan issues)
6. No monitoring during test
7. One-off runs (should be repeatable, comparable)
8. Only happy path (stress error paths too)
9. No SLOs ('is this fast enough?' with no answer)
10. Optimization without measurement (guess; prove it)

**Strategic considerations**

*Coordinated vs uncoordinated omission*
- Most tools (JMeter default, naive k6) suffer coordinated omission
- When request takes long, subsequent not sent until done; hides latency
- Use open model: Gatling open, k6 constant-arrival-rate, wrk2
- Otherwise p99 dramatically optimistic

*Java-specific*
- JIT warmup: 1-2 min low load before measurement
- GC tuning: pause is major outlier contributor
- Low-latency: G1 (default), ZGC, Shenandoah (sub-ms pauses on large heaps)
- Tune Xms = Xmx (avoid resize)
- GC time > 5% CPU = problematic
- Virtual threads (JDK 21+, Spring Boot 3.2+): game-changer for IO-bound; test both platform and virtual
- HikariCP default 10 often too low for high RPS; tune via heuristic; watch pendingThreads metric

**Capacity planning**
- Test at expected load × 1.5-2x (growth + safety)
- Capacity ≠ max throughput; capacity = max at acceptable latency
- Use to size infra and set autoscaler thresholds

**Microservices**
- Test individual services in isolation
- Then test critical flows end-to-end
- Identify which services bottleneck first
- Slow downstream cascades; bulkheads/breakers prevent

**Database load**
- DB is most common bottleneck in high-RPS
- Realistic data volume + distribution; not 1000 rows
- Watch query plans (Postgres EXPLAIN ANALYZE)
- Connection pool sizing critical at DB (max_connections) and app (HikariCP)
- Read replicas, caching, denormalization, async writes

**Cache effects**
- First N requests fill cache; subsequent hit; latency drops
- Decide: cold or warm cache test?
- Cache eviction under load can cause sudden spikes

**Production validation**
- Synthetic monitoring continuously runs key flows in prod
- RUM captures actual user latency
- Some perf bugs only show in production traffic patterns
- Canary deploys with extra monitoring catch perf regressions before full rollout

**Not one-time**
- Continuous: every merge runs smoke
- Periodic: full load on releases
- Pre-event: extra capacity tests before known spikes (Black Friday, campaigns)
- Reactive: when perf incident, reproduce + fix

**Strategic take**
- Pick right test type for question
- Define SLOs first; measure against
- Prod-like env with prod-like data
- Profile + observe during, not just at end
- Iterate on bottlenecks, one at a time
- Embrace continuous perf testing like unit tests
- Tail latency is what users feel; p99/p99.9 is the real number

**Bottom line**
- Performance testing is engineering discipline, not occasional ritual
- The right tool, the right data, the right environment, the right metrics
- Measure, hypothesize, fix, re-measure

speakable_v2.standard_example: Spring Boot service class tested with JUnit 5 and Mockito
